newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK REFERENCE BANKS SAID TO AGREE VOLUME CUT.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK REFERENCE BANKS SAID TO AGREE VOLUME CUT.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) and eight reference banks on the money market have agreed to a temporary cut in their minimum quoted volumes in the face of interest rate volatity, dealers said on Wednesday.

"Until recalled, the reference banks will continue to cumpulsorily quote currently lower volumes, by half, due to worries of the interest rate volatility, which may follow the current liquidity outflow," Martin Hrozany, chief dealer at Slovenska Sporitelna, told Reuters.

The decision is an outcome of a meeting of the reference banks' on Tuesday, which had been called to reassess the cut in compulsory quoted volumes for one month from January 15, which prompted by an acute liquidity shortage.
Under the agreement, dealers said maturities of two and three months have a minimum volume of 50 million crowns, while four to six month terms have a 25 million crown minimum volume.

Reference banks must provide bid/offer quotations for standard deposit maturities, with a set spread, and must have certain minimum credit lines as well as minimum trading volumes for other market participants.
Quotations from the eight banks are used to determine the Bratislava Interbank Offered Rate (BRIBOR).
Rates from three to six months are most commonly used to determine the instruments such as swaps and forwards.

"Some banks appear scared of a liquidity insufficiency or uncertainty, but I think the agreement itself adds to uncertainty. Thus it is a mistake to quote lower volumes," said Rastislav Zivor, a dealer with ING Bank.

The liquidity cruch, which had prompted the agreement along with a boost in Slovak interbank money market rates to record highs of 26 percent in January, was soon relaxed by an inflow of estimated $130-380 million since then.
On Tuesday, the NBS said that most of the inflow had already been pulled out of Slovakia.
Interbank money market rates rose on Wednesday the average 150 basis points on short terms, and some 50 basis points on longer to a range of 17.5-19 percent, flattening the yield curve.
Dealers said they expected the rise to level out at a 20 percent level due to the outflow, while eyeing the central bank for some kind of interest rate intervention.
